newsitem.title: UK: Moody's rates Kazakhstan foreign currency Ba3.
newsitem.headline: Moody's rates Kazakhstan foreign currency Ba3.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Monday it assigned a Ba3 sovereign ceiling for ratings on long-term foreign-currency bonds and notes of issuers domicilied in Kazakhstan.
"Accordingly, Moody's expects to assign a Ba3 to the forthcoming Eurobond issue of the Republic of Kazakhstan," Moody's said in a statement.

"In line with its view that bank deposits are generally riskier obligations than bonds, the rating agency also assigned a B1 sovereign ceiling for ratings of foreign currency-denominated bank deposits."
Moody's also assigned Not Prime ceilings for short-term notes and bank deposits.
Moody's said Kazakhstan is basing its future on political stability, enshrined in a strong presidency, and increased exploitation of considerable raw material wealth.

"The Republic's surfeit of natural resources has already attracted foreign direct investment and led to solid export earnings. These, in turn, have boosted external liquidity so that reserves now cover three to four months of imports."
Moody's said it will monitor Kazakstan's future development closely in light of the republic's ability to attract considerable foreign direct investment.

"A key focus will be the government's continued commitment to tight fiscal and monetary policies in the event that a significant surge in foreign direct investment generates foreign exchange reserves and budgetary revenues that provide the wherewithal for greater social expenditures, infrastructural provision, and international borrowing," the agency said.

The dissolution of the Soviet Union left Kazakhstan with no international debt, it said, and although the rate at which it has accumluated debt in the past five years is significant, overall external and internal debt ratios remain modest.
Moody's said Kazakhstan's medium-term problems lie --
-- in its relationship with Russia, which is pursuing a fairly blatant policy of economic imperialism towards Kazakhstan,
-- in its low domestic savings rate, which could constrain future investments,
-- in its inadequate tax code and inefficient tax collection system, which are forcing unhealthy spending cuts in efforts to contain the budget deficit,

-- and in its slow approach to enterprise and banking sector reform, including the related issue of substantial interenterprise arrears, which at some point could imperil tight fiscal and monetary policy.
